questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: locate a warrant that the argument states outright
questions.stem: A district note reads: 'Inspection failures in our restaurants are caused by grease, not by small kitchens: every restaurant that failed last year had grease-thick hood filters, and a restaurant whose filters are cleaned monthly has never failed. Grease builds up whenever filters go unchecked, so any kitchen can stay out of the failure list by cleaning them monthly.' Which clause states the warrant?

options.text: Grease builds up whenever filters go unchecked
Every restaurant that failed last year had grease-thick hood filters
options.misconception: names a specific observation, which is the reason offered rather than the rule

options.text: A restaurant whose filters are cleaned monthly has never failed
options.misconception: treats a second observation as though it were the linking general rule

options.text: Any kitchen can stay out of the failure list by cleaning them monthly
options.misconception: reads the recommendation raised by the warrant as the warrant itself

questions.explanation: A warrant is the general statement that makes the move from a reason to a claim, and only one clause here is general rather than particular: the word whenever makes 'grease builds up' a rule about all filters, not a report about one kitchen. Clauses B and C are the two observations a reader can count, which is exactly what evidence does in an argument. Clause D is what the argument asks the reader to do, so it is the claim the warrant supports rather than the warrant.
questions.hint: Ask which clause would still be true of a kitchen that is not in the district.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Arguable claims and matters of fact
questions.learningObjective: separate a matter of fact from a sentence that only looks factual
questions.stem: A residents' group sends a letter with four sentences. Which of the four states a matter of fact?

options.text: 'The branch library in this district opened in 1974.'
'Our branch should stay open on Sundays all year.'
options.misconception: asks a decision to be made, so it can be argued rather than checked

options.text: 'Weekend staffing has been thin at the branch for two years.'
options.misconception: treats the evaluative word thin as though it were a countable measure

options.text: 'The nearest branch open on Sunday is a two-hour trip by bus.'
options.misconception: assumes the trip time is a matter of judgment when it can be looked up

questions.explanation: A matter of fact is settled by looking something up, and an opening year is exactly that: a reader can confirm 1974 in the council's record or fail to. Sentence B is a request, so it is the arguable claim of the letter. Sentence C is the trap in this item, because 'thin' carries a judgment inside a sentence shaped like a measurement, and sentence D is a distance and a timetable that a reader can check just as directly as the year.
questions.hint: Look for the sentence with no evaluating word and nothing to decide.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify where an argument's conclusion rests on a stipulated term
questions.stem: A school board's notice reads: 'From March, any student who leaves school grounds during the day must have written parental consent on file. A student who leaves the campus without permission is truant, and reducing truancy is what our attendance policy was written to do.' The board argues from a definition. Where does the argument get its conclusion?

options.text: From sorting each case of leaving into the class the policy already names
From counting how often students left the grounds before the rule existed
options.misconception: answers with a count the notice never supplies

options.text: From comparing the new rule with those used at neighbouring schools
options.misconception: switches to a comparison the notice never makes

options.text: From assuming that each absent student meant to miss school on purpose
options.misconception: adds a motive that the definition of truant does not contain

questions.explanation: An argument by definition decides a case by placing it inside a term the writer has already fixed, and the notice does exactly that: it says a student who leaves without permission is truant, then treats reducing truancy as the standing aim of the policy. The rule follows from the classification rather than from any measurement. Nothing in the passage counts past behaviour, compares other schools, or assigns motives, so options B, C and D each add a move the text does not make.
questions.hint: Ask what the word truant is doing for the rule that follows it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the disanalogy that weakens a comparison used as support
questions.stem: A council debate runs like this: 'Our seed library has worked for six years from a converted telephone box, so the council should run a repair café from the same box.' A councillor objects: 'The two are not alike in what they need.' Which difference the objector names is the one that weakens the analogy most?

options.text: A repair café needs power, a bench and supervision on site
The seed library has run for six years without a complaint
options.misconception: cites length of success, which supports the analogy instead of breaking it

options.text: The seed library opens on the same weekday the council meets
options.misconception: reports a scheduling detail that has no bearing on the comparison

options.text: The box belongs to the council rather than to a volunteer group
options.misconception: names who owns the building, which is not a difference in use

questions.explanation: An analogy is only as strong as the likeness it needs, and the objector attacks exactly where the two cases differ in what they require. A seed library hands something over and closes, while a repair café needs tools, a power supply and a person responsible while visitors work, so the box that suits the first may not suit the second at all. Option B is the record of the analogy working, and options C and D are details of ownership and calendar that the comparison never depends on.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the two operations needs in order to happen at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: decide when citing an expert is a support rather than an appeal to authority
questions.stem: Four writers back a claim with someone else's authority. In which case is the appeal to authority doing legitimate work?

options.text: A claim about rainfall totals backed by a published measurement from a weather service
A claim about a balanced diet backed by a novelist's advice to friends
options.misconception: treats any named person as competent on a question they write about, not one they study

options.text: A claim about tax rates backed by a general's view from a military briefing
options.misconception: counts rank in one field as expertise in a different one

options.text: A claim about a product's safety backed by the firm's own engineer on the payroll
options.misconception: accepts self-certification from a party that gains from the verdict

questions.explanation: Citing an authority is legitimate when the claim falls inside what that authority is competent to know and the cited work stands behind the claim, which is what a weather service's published rainfall totals do for a claim about rainfall. Option B gives a writer of fiction no standing in nutrition, and option C borrows the general's standing in one domain for a question in another. Option D is worse than irrelevance, because the certifying engineer is paid by the party the verdict would help.
questions.hint: Ask whether the cited person works in the field the claim is about.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: recognise an argument that reasons from what a position would produce
questions.stem: A fund's chair writes: 'Do not accept the scholarship's conditions. If word gets out that our money comes with strings attached, donors will stop giving, and the programme dies within a year.' What makes this an argument from consequence rather than a reason for the claim?

options.text: The support offered is what will follow if the position is taken
The support offered is a record of how donors have already behaved
options.misconception: reads a predicted consequence as an observation already made

options.text: The claim is a rule the writer says donors have always followed
options.misconception: mistakes the writer's expectation for a stated rule of donors' conduct

options.misconception: treats a silence as if it were the shape of the reasoning

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: report what a precedent covers and what a case does with it
questions.stem: A council debate reads: 'We paved the shared path at Elm Park in 2019, and reported falls on it have fallen every year since. Last winter a resident asked us to pave the path behind her building. The Elm Park path is our precedent, and the request in front of us is the case.' First state what the precedent covers, then state what the case does with it.

options.text: One paved path and its reported falls, applied to a second path as a question
Every unpaved path in the district, which settles them all at once
options.misconception: inflates one completed case into a district-wide rule the passage never states

options.text: The cost of paving in 2019, weighed against this year's budget
options.misconception: moves the precedent from results to spending, which the passage never mentions

options.text: The opinions of the two walkers quoted, which the council must choose between
options.misconception: invents testimony the debate does not contain

questions.explanation: An argument from precedent uses one settled case to license a later one, and here the writer names both ends himself: the Elm Park path is the precedent and the request before the council is the case. What the precedent covers is therefore one path's paving and its record of reported falls, and what the case does with it is raise the same treatment for a different path as a question the council still has to answer. Option B pretends one case already decides every path, and option C substitutes a cost comparison the passage does not make.
questions.hint: Find the two things the speaker labels as precedent and as case.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: choose the observation that would confirm a claim stated at a wider scope
questions.stem: A council minute reads: 'Crashes at the goods depot fell by half in the year after the flashing beacon was installed. A second count of crashes at the depot crossing for the next year
options.misconception: adds evidence for the one site the minute already covers

options.text: A survey of drivers reporting that the beacon feels safer to pass
options.misconception: substitutes a feeling reported by drivers for a measured rate

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain why evidence can be relevant and still not enough
questions.stem: Advocates write: 'The town should build a covered shelter at the school gate. One hundred and eighty students use that gate, and rain was recorded on sixty of the last ninety school days.' Both figures are true. Why is the evidence relevant but not yet sufficient?

options.text: It counts rain and foot traffic but never the waiting itself
It uses ninety days where the claim needs a whole year
options.misconception: asks for a longer count although no yearly claim is made

options.text: It leaves out the wind and cold the passage also mentions
options.misconception: invents weather conditions that the passage never lists

options.text: It gives a headcount of students but no count of buses
options.misconception: demands a bus count on which the claim never depends

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of a reply that confronts a counterargument
questions.stem: A writer is about to answer an objection to a claim about a new bus timetable. Put the four moves in the order that makes the reply answerable rather than merely forceful.

options.text: Restate your own claim once the objection has been dealt with
options.misconception: puts the writer's own claim first, before the reader can see what is being answered

options.text: Give the objection's strongest reason, in the form its best advocate would use
options.misconception: answers a weak version of the objection, which no reader was making

options.text: Show why that reason does not hold, using the claim's own evidence
options.misconception: declines to answer and moves straight to restating the claim

options.text: Name the counterclaim a reasonable reader could make against you
options.misconception: starts the reply with a conclusion, before the objection exists on the page

questions.explanation: A reply is checkable only if the reader can see what is being answered, so the counterclaim has to be named first and then stated in the strongest form its best advocate would recognise. Only after the reason is fairly stated can the writer show that it fails, and restating the claim last confirms that the objection was answered rather than dodged. Starting with the claim or with the defeat of the objection leaves the reader without the thing being answered, which is why those orders read as force rather than argument.
questions.hint: Nothing can be answered until the reader can see what the objection is.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain why strong evidence can still fail to bear on a claim
questions.stem: A tenant's letter says: 'The landlord must repair the boiler before winter, and the boiler was last serviced in 2014, which is the year the manufacturer changed the parts it uses.' Why is the second piece of evidence strong but irrelevant?

options.text: It is true and precise but concerns parts, not the boiler's condition
It is true but too old to be used in a letter about repairs
options.misconception: dismisses a dated fact although dates are what the letter relies on

options.text: It is too precise, and a tenant's letter should use general terms
options.misconception: objects to precision in a document whose whole case is dates and records

options.text: It is irrelevant because no other tenant has mentioned the same year
options.misconception: requires a second tenant's report, which the letter never needed

questions.explanation: Strength and relevance are different properties. The date of a parts change is checkable and may be perfectly accurate, but the letter's claim is about the boiler's condition and what the landlord should do about it, and a change in spare-part design bears on neither. This is the trap that catches careful writers: the better the sourcing, the more convincing the irrelevance looks. Options B, C and D each reject the fact for reasons that have nothing to do with whether it supports the demand.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim is about, then whether the fact is about that.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name the warrant a writer assumes without stating
questions.stem: A letter to a college says: 'Our sixth-form results rose for four years running while class sizes fell, so the smaller classes are why the results rose.' Which reason does the letter leave unstated?

options.text: That class size is what affects results, not something alongside it
That four years is long enough to show a real change
options.misconception: names a question about time, which the letter never raises

options.text: That the college is free to set class sizes at will
options.misconception: raises a question about control the letter does not need

options.text: That the results are measured by the same test each year
options.misconception: adds a question about measurement the letter takes for granted elsewhere

questions.explanation: Two things rose and fell together over four years, which gives the letter an association but not a cause, and the step from association to cause is exactly the unstated reason. The warrant is that class size is the operative variable here, that smaller groups produce the improvement rather than merely travelling alongside it. Options B, C and D each identify a question a reader might ask, but none of them is the reasoning the conclusion needs, which is why challenging them would leave the argument standing.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be true, and not merely observed, for the conclusion to follow.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: spot the word that turns a claim into an easier one
questions.stem: A councillor replies to a proposal for a bus gate: 'Nobody is arguing against safe buses. Anyone who opposes a bus gate wants buses unsafe, and once we admit that, the case for more speed limits is settled.' Which word gives away the move being made?

options.text: Anyone, which turns a qualified preference into a belief about all
Nobody, which denies that anyone holds the position at all
options.misconception: reads the opening as a claim about the absence of opponents, which is not its work

options.text: Unsafe, which repeats the council's own word without adding a claim
options.misconception: thinks the giveaway word is the one the speaker repeats from the proposal

options.text: Settled, which reports a decision the council has in fact reached
options.misconception: reads the closing word as a description of a completed vote

questions.explanation: A straw man replaces the opponent's claim with a stronger and less defensible one, and the word doing that work is 'anyone': it converts an argument about which buses may use a street into a position on bus safety altogether, which nobody who proposed a time-limited gate is obliged to hold. Once the easier claim is defeated, the speaker treats the original as settled too, which is the second half of the trick. Option B misreads the opening as a claim that no opponents exist, and options C and D attach the giveaway to words that are not altering the claim.
questions.hint: Find the word that widens the opponent's position beyond what it said.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: supply the premise a conclusion needs and the passage withholds
questions.stem: A claim in a report reads: 'The new evening bus has not improved punctuality on the Ridgeway, so the corridor does not need a second bus.' What must be true for that conclusion to follow, and is it stated anywhere in the report?

options.text: That one bus is the only way to improve punctuality, and the report does not state it
That evening passengers are content with the current timetable, and the report says so
options.misconception: invents a report finding about passenger contentment that the claim never used

options.text: That punctuality is the only measure of a bus service, and the report limits it to that
options.misconception: supplies a restriction the report never imposed on itself

options.text: That a second bus was tried before and failed, which the report sets out
options.misconception: describes a second trial that the report does not record

questions.explanation: One bus failing to improve punctuality shows that this bus, on its own, did not do it, and the conclusion needs the stronger premise that no other intervention could. That premise is a claim about the whole field of options, and nothing in the quoted sentence supplies it, which is the hidden premise the report never states. Option B invents a finding, option C narrows the report's own measure without warrant, and option D adds a trial that the report does not record, so none of them fills the gap the conclusion needs.
questions.hint: Ask whether one failure of one option rules out every other option.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a counterargument takes on the claim or the person
questions.stem: An opponent of a library closure writes: 'The person proposing this closure has never worked in a library, and the plan was drafted by someone who admits reading one report.' Why does that sentence fail as a counterargument?

It gives two separate arguments and neither is finished
options.misconception: treats a single attack on credentials as though it were two claims

options.text: It attacks the evidence and so ignores the writer's conclusion
options.misconception: mistakes a complaint about reading for an argument about evidence

options.text: It is too short to establish a case against a public plan
options.misconception: objects to length, which is not what makes a rebuttal work

Option C misreads the reading complaint as a dispute about evidence, and option D makes length the test, which it is not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the structure of an argument that diverts from its own claim
questions.stem: A writer arguing for a new bus shelter writes: 'The council cut the grass verge twice this year instead of once, which shows how little the verges matter to anybody.' The paragraph never returns to the shelter. What has happened structurally?

The supporting detail has been dropped and the conclusion kept
options.misconception: reverses what happened, since the conclusion is what disappears

options.misconception: claims more evidence was added, when the mowing figures replaced it

options.text: The claim has been narrowed to the length of a single season
options.misconception: describes a restriction on scope, which the paragraph never states

Option B has the two reversed, and options C and D describe work the paragraph does not do.

questions.learningObjective: name the second causal claim a post hoc inference leaves open
questions.stem: A clinic reports: 'Appointments fell by half in the six months after we began sending reminder texts, so the texts halved our no-shows.' Which other causal claim does that sentence leave open, and why does it matter?

options.text: That bookings were falling in those months whatever the texts did
That texts went only to patients who attend most often
options.misconception: supplies a selection effect the clinic never mentions

options.text: That the texts cost more than the missed visits saved
options.misconception: turns a claim of effect into a question of cost

options.text: That the falling count covered cancellations, not no-shows
options.misconception: switches the category the report's figure never used

questions.explanation: The report fixes a time, six months, and a change, half as many appointments, and then treats the interval as the cause. But a falling count over the same six months is exactly what a falling trend, a season, or a change in opening hours would also produce, and the report cannot tell those apart from its own texts. The unstated rival claim is not a guess about the patients; it is the ordinary possibility that the number would have dropped anyway. That is why the wording 'in the six months after' is the weakest phrase in the sentence.
questions.hint: Ask what else could have produced the same fall in those same months.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: explain why the order of two events does not establish a cause
questions.stem: A committee reports: 'The warning light was switched on in March. In April the fault that had gone unresolved for two years disappeared, and the machine has run without it since. The light did what it should.' What makes this an argument from what came first?

options.text: It treats March coming before April as the cause of the change
It claims the machine ran worse, which the report never measures
options.misconception: denies a performance claim that the report does not make

options.text: It rests on the committee's own account of how the fault was fixed
options.misconception: reads the report as depending on testimony nobody offers

options.text: It doubts the machine ran at all during the first two years
options.misconception: questions the earlier history the report accepts

questions.explanation: Everything the report offers is sequence: the light in March, the fault gone in April, no fault since. Sequence is not cause, and the argument needs one more thing, which is a reason the light should have been what changed the machine's behaviour. A repair carried out in the same March, or a new part fitted at the same visit, would produce the same April. The phrase 'did what it should' is the report asserting the link rather than showing it, which is the whole of the fault.
questions.hint: Ask what else the committee did in March.

questions.learningObjective: locate the missing intermediate step in a chain of consequences
questions.stem: A speaker says: 'If we allow one late licence on the corner, the next request will be for a licence every night, then for a bar, then for a nightclub, and in ten years the high street will be a strip of them.' Which step in the chain is doing the unargued work?

From a licence every night to a bar on the same corner
options.misconception: picks a later link although the first jump is the one unargued

options.text: From the corner's first licence to the state of the street
options.misconception: objects to the timescale, which the speaker offered as a rough figure

options.text: From a bar to a nightclub, which changes the use of the building
options.misconception: treats a later link as though it were the unargued one

questions.explanation: A chain of consequences is only as strong as its weakest link, and this one jumps at the start. Once that first step is missing, the later ones float free of it, which is why the speaker's ten-year strip of venues is not a conclusion but a picture. questions.hint: Find the first jump, not the most dramatic one.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: recognise a reason that restates the claim in other words
questions.stem: A speaker says: 'We know the plan is fair because a fair plan is one that treats every household the same, and this plan treats every household the same, so it is fair.' What has the sentence done with the question it was answering?

options.text: It used the word fair in the reason it gave for fairness
It gave a rule a reader could check against the household list
options.misconception: treats a checkable rule as though it were an independent reason

options.text: It compared two plans and found this one the more even
options.misconception: invents a comparison the sentence never makes

options.text: It conceded the plan is not fair and answered that objection
options.misconception: supposes a concession the speaker never makes

questions.explanation: The middle clause sounds like help because it defines fairness, and a definition does look like something a reader can use. But 'a fair plan is one that treats every household the same' puts the word being questioned inside the reason given for it, so the argument settles what it was asked and never reaches anything outside itself. The sameness of treatment is exactly what is at issue, and a plan can treat every household identically and still be unfair if the households are not alike. That is the difference between a reason and a restatement.
questions.hint: Look for the word that appears in the claim and in its own justification.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify a conclusion that runs against the reason offered for it
questions.stem: A report argues: 'Fewer than a third of the town's commuters now cycle, and every main route has two steep hills on it, so the town does not need a cycle network.' Which part does not follow?

options.text: The conclusion, because the hills given as the cause argue for a network
The figure, because a third is high for a town with hills
options.misconception: reverses the judgment the figure actually supports

options.text: The count of hills, because two are too few to explain the number
options.misconception: disputes a count the report never treats as decisive

options.text: The word commuters, because it includes people who travel by bus
options.misconception: invents a counting practice the report never mentions

questions.explanation: The reason and the conclusion pull in opposite directions. If steep hills are what keeps people off bikes, then a network that used the routes least obstructed by hills would be the remedy the reason points at, and the low number becomes evidence for building one. A conclusion that follows from the reason would be that this town's hills make a network expensive to plan, not unnecessary. That is what a non sequitur looks like from the inside: the writer finds a reason, stops reasoning, and states whatever the topic suggests.
questions.hint: Ask which way the stated reason points.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name the faults in a short letter and state what the causal claim still needs
questions.stem: A school letter argues: 'Our results have risen for four years running, so the new tracking programme caused the rise. Tracking only shows staff where each pupil stands, so anyone who doubts the programme is resisting evidence.' In three to four sentences, name the two faults in this letter and say what the writer would have to add to make the causal claim arguable.

answer.exemplar: The first fault is a post hoc claim: a rise over four years and a programme introduced somewhere in them do not make the programme the cause, and the letter offers nothing that would separate the two. The second fault is a dismissal of critics rather than a reply to them, since it treats doubt as an attitude instead of a reason. To be arguable the letter needs comparison, meaning results for comparable groups without tracking over the same years, or a change in results in the years since tracking began against the years before.

questions.explanation: Two things are wrong and they are wrong in different ways, so a response that merges them will be vague. The causal claim needs the rival explanation removed, which only a comparison can do, and the sentence about doubt needs its second term fixed, because a reader who doubts the programme may simply have asked what the comparison shows. A good answer names the post hoc inference, names the attack on the doubter, and specifies the comparison that would settle the cause.
questions.hint: One fault is in the cause, the other in the reply to people who disagree.

questions.learningObjective: identify the appeal to authority that cites an expert in the wrong field
questions.stem: A resident argues: 'The library should not close on Sundays, because a doctor I know says children need somewhere quiet at the weekend, and doctors know more about children than librarians do.' What is the fault in the appeal?

A librarian should have been cited, and not a doctor
options.misconception: insists on one profession where the test is fit between claim and field

options.text: A doctor who knows children would be right to want more weekend space
options.misconception: accepts the comparison of expertise as a way to settle opening hours

options.text: The doctor's view counts for less because the resident is not a parent
options.misconception: makes the speaker's own standing the thing under question

questions.hint: Ask what subject the claim is about, and then whether the cited person works in it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: state what decides whether an argument is valid
questions.stem: An argument runs: 'Every late return recorded at this desk was made by a reading room member, and sixty per cent of all returns were late. So sixty per cent of reading room members returned books late.' What decides whether that conclusion follows?

options.text: Whether the figure in the premise is drawn from the group the conclusion names
Whether the argument names a source a reader could go and check
options.misconception: treats checkability as though it were the condition of validity

options.text: Whether the conclusion happens to be true in this library
options.misconception: makes truth in the world the test of an inference

options.text: Whether the two groups contain the same number of members
options.misconception: requires equal sizes, which validity has never needed

questions.explanation: Validity is decided by shape alone: if the premises are true, must the conclusion be? Here the answer is no, and the fault is visible in the word all. Sixty per cent of all returns is a share of every return, while the conclusion converts it into a share of reading room members, a group the premise says nothing about in proportion. No reader can check the figures to rescue it, because the shape is wrong whatever the figures turn out to be, and its truth in this library is a separate question that validity never asks.
questions.hint: Compare the group the percentage is taken from with the group it is assigned to.

questions.learningObjective: test a summary's claim about a passage against what the passage contains

A quotation from a caretaker who runs the hall on weekdays

options.misconception: invents the comparison the summary describes

questions.stem: A landlord says: 'Nobody here is being evicted unfairly, because unfair eviction is not something this tenancy can involve.' What has the sentence done with the objection?

It gave a reason about the tenancy that the tenant could check
options.misconception: reads a definition as though it were an independent reason

options.text: It compared this tenancy with the other flats in the block
options.misconception: invents a comparison the sentence does not make

The sentence defines unfairness so narrowly that it excludes this case, and the exclusion is then announced as a finding, so a tenant who has been given notice without notice being valid has been told their experience is a category error rather than answered. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of an argument by contradiction
questions.stem: A writer wants to dispose of a claim by showing it cannot be true. Put the four moves of the argument in the order they must come in.

options.text: Draw out the consequence and show it is one no defender can accept
options.misconception: produces a consequence before the claim has been granted

options.text: Assume the claim, granting its premises for the sake of the argument
options.misconception: starts from a consequence with nothing granted

options.text: Conclude the claim cannot stand, since it leads where it leads
options.misconception: concludes before the consequence has been shown

options.text: Take the strongest form of the claim, not the weakest one
options.misconception: grants a claim the writer has weakened in advance

questions.explanation: This form of refutation works by granting and then taking, so the order is fixed. The claim is stated in its strongest form first, because a contradiction that defeats a weak version defeats nothing; next it is granted, premises and all, which is what entitles the writer to derive anything at all. The consequence comes third and has to be one the defender cannot accept without giving up the claim they are defending, and only then does the conclusion follow. Starting at the consequence would leave the reader unable to see what was assumed, and granting the weakest version wastes the refutation.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer is entitled to assume, and when.

It shows the scheme is lawful, which settles what residents raised
options.misconception: treats procedure as though it settled the effect

options.text: It admits the free spaces will go and offers a replacement instead

options.misconception: takes the quoting of a document for the answering of a claim

questions.learningObjective: separate a conclusion that happens to be true from the reasoning offered for it
questions.stem: An argument runs: 'The new bus route has been running for a year, and the town has had no rail strike in that year, so the route is what stopped the strike.' The conclusion happens to be true. What is still wrong?

The conclusion is false, since a bus could not stop a strike
options.misconception: denies a conclusion the question states is true

options.text: The premises are too few, and one more would have to be added
options.misconception: counts premises rather than judging the link between them

options.text: The argument is valid, since its conclusion is the one that is true
options.misconception: treats truth in the world as making an inference correct

questions.explanation: A conclusion can be right for reasons the argument never gives, and when that happens the reasoning is the thing a reader still has to distrust. Truth in the world and correctness in the argument come apart, and only the second is what validity is about.

questions.learningObjective: sequence the questions a reader puts to an argument

options.misconception: asks for a test before the claim has been identified

options.text: Ask what claim is being made
options.misconception: starts with a challenge that has nothing yet to attach to

options.misconception: asks for support before the claim is known

questions.topic: The reason that does the work
questions.learningObjective: identify which sentence supplies the connection the argument really needs
questions.stem: A letter says: 'We are short of parking spaces, which is why the market should move to the edge of town. Traders at that site already sell well in the open, so the move would suit them.' Which sentence is doing the real work?

options.text: The second, which supplies the comparison the parking complaint lacks
The first, which names the shortage the market would relieve
options.misconception: credits the stated problem with a link it cannot make

questions.learningObjective: locate the arguable part of a claim dressed as a statistic
questions.stem: A council's survey summary reads: 'Ninety per cent of the two hundred and forty residents who answered are satisfied with the service, and satisfaction is what a service meeting its need looks like, so the service meets its need.' Which part cannot be settled by counting?

options.text: The claim that satisfaction is what a met need looks like
The figure of ninety per cent, which is a matter of record
options.misconception: picks the countable part as though it were the arguable one

options.text: The sample of two hundred and forty, which might have been larger
options.misconception: attacks the sample where the question is about the claim

options.text: The word service, which covers more than the survey asked about
options.misconception: makes a scope complaint the survey figures do not raise

questions.learningObjective: identify the term traded between two senses in a short argument
questions.stem: A college argues: 'The year abroad is a learning experience, and experience comes only from doing things, so students should spend the year in the workshop rather than in lectures.' Which term has been traded between two senses?

options.text: Learning, which means study in one clause and a gain from practice
Experience, which means an event in one clause and a skill in the other
options.misconception: gives a second sense to a word the argument uses steadily

options.text: Doing, which means action in one clause and a method in the other
options.misconception: shifts a word that stays with action throughout

options.text: Course, which means a programme in one clause and a set of classes
options.misconception: invents a distinction the argument never makes

questions.topic: The third option in a dilemma
questions.learningObjective: identify what would show a two-way choice is not exhaustive
questions.stem: A landlord tells a tenant: 'Raise the rent to the new figure or move out, and there is no third option.' What would show the third option is not empty?

How many other tenants the landlord has in the building

options.text: How long the tenant has lived in the flat
options.misconception: supplies a length of stay the choice does not turn on

questions.learningObjective: identify a disputed premise presented as ground both sides hold
questions.stem: An argument runs: 'Both sides accept that the road must be widened, so the only question left is where the money comes from.' What has the argument done with the dispute?

options.text: Moved one side's claim into shared ground, so the real dispute has gone
Found the only question left once both claims are granted
options.misconception: takes the narrowing at face value

options.text: Moved the argument to a question both sides can be trusted on
options.misconception: supposes a shared question the argument does not offer

options.text: Left the easier question aside in order to take up the harder
options.misconception: reads avoidance as a deliberate strategy

questions.learningObjective: distinguish evidence of difficulty from evidence of impossibility
questions.stem: A writer says: 'The scheme cannot work, because there is no money for it and nobody wants it.' A reader answers: 'Both may be true, and it may still be the right thing to do next year.' What has the writer's reasoning failed to establish?

options.text: That the scheme cannot work, rather than that it is hard to fund now
That the money is missing, which the reader has not denied
options.misconception: reads the reader's hedge as a dispute about the figures

options.text: That nobody wants it, which the writer has only asserted
options.misconception: treats an assertion as something the reader conceded

options.text: That next year will bring the same figures, which nobody knows
options.misconception: supplies a forecast that neither side made

questions.explanation: Two facts about this year are being converted into a claim about every year, and the word cannot is where the conversion happens. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the unexamined event that would produce a result without the claimed cause
questions.stem: A trader says: 'I moved the stall to the corner by the station, takings rose by a third, and that corner is what did it.' The station car park, three hundred yards away, closed for repairs in the same month. What has the trader not examined?

options.text: A change at the station that would lift takings wherever the stall stood
A rival stall that closed in the same month as the move
options.misconception: invents a competitor the passage never mentions

options.text: A rise in the price of the goods sold that month
options.misconception: supplies a price change the passage records nowhere

options.text: A shorter trading day, which would have lowered takings
options.misconception: supplies a change that works against the claim

questions.explanation: Closing a car park moves people out of their cars and onto foot at exactly the moment the trader moved, and a stall that intercepts footfall would take a share of that whether it stood at the corner or three hundred yards away. What is missing is not a statistic but a separation, since the two changes cannot be told apart in a single month of takings.

options.misconception: measures other towns rather than this service's record

questions.learningObjective: state what makes a cited authority usable support
questions.stem: A council argues it can run the depot itself, citing a report signed by an engineer who has run three comparable depots, with the staffing plan and the throughput estimate set out in full. Why is this different from citing a name?

An engineer's signature settles a question about running a depot
options.misconception: treats the document's existence as evidence for its contents

options.misconception: counts experience as though it removed the need to check

options.misconception: supplies a link between two figures the report does not join

questions.topic: A warrant the writer has not noticed
questions.learningObjective: state a hidden premise and what accepting it commits a writer to
questions.stem: An argument runs: 'The hall's roof is slate, slate roofs are heavy, so the hall needs a bigger crew to inspect it.' First state the unstated premise, then say what it commits the writer to.

options.text: That crew size follows weight, and that inspection is the work affected
That slate is heavier than tile, and that the hall has a slate roof
options.misconception: names the two facts the argument already states

options.text: That the crew is paid by the hour, and that the hall is council-owned
options.misconception: supplies facts about pay and ownership the argument never uses

options.text: That slate outlasts tile, and that a long roof needs less work
options.misconception: reverses the relation the word heavy sets up

questions.learningObjective: name what two compared cases share and where they differ

The same number of rooms, and the age of the hall's roof
options.misconception: supplies a physical detail the comparison never turns on

options.misconception: compares budgets where the argument needs dependence

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the parts of a short argument so each one supports the next
questions.stem: A writer is turning three notes into a short argument. Put the four parts in the order that makes each one support the next.

options.text: Say what follows for the reader, so the argument has a point
options.misconception: arrives at a consequence before the claim is stated

options.text: State the claim, so the reader knows what is being argued
options.misconception: puts the conclusion first and asks for support afterwards

options.text: Offer the reason for it, so the claim has something under it
options.misconception: offers a reason before the claim it is a reason for

options.text: Give the rule that connects the reason to the claim
options.misconception: supplies the connecting rule before the two ends it joins

questions.explanation: The parts have a dependency order and the order is not a matter of taste. The claim comes first, because a reader who does not know what is being argued cannot weigh anything else; the reason follows, since a reason is a reason for something. The rule connecting them comes third, and this is the move writers skip, so the reason and the claim sit side by side with a so between them and nothing inside. Only when all three are in place can the last sentence say what follows, because what follows is a consequence of the claim as argued rather than a wish attached to it.
questions.hint: Ask which part each of the others exists to serve.
